text: The available evidence on vitamin D and mortality was inconclusive. The review aimed to assess the beneficial and harmful effects of vitamin D for preventing mortality in adults.

The search covered The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, the Science Citation Index Expanded, and Conference Proceedings Citation Index-Science. The authors also scanned bibliographies and asked experts and pharmaceutical companies for additional trials.

The review included randomized trials that compared vitamin D at any dose, duration, and route of administration against placebo or no intervention. Vitamin D could be administered as vitamin D3, vitamin D2, alfacalcidol, or calcitriol.

Fifty randomized trials with 94,148 participants provided mortality data. Overall, vitamin D slightly decreased mortality. When different forms were assessed separately, only vitamin D3 significantly decreased mortality, whereas vitamin D2, alfacalcidol, and calcitriol did not.

Vitamin D3 combined with calcium increased the risk of nephrolithiasis. Alfacalcidol and calcitriol increased the risk of hypercalcaemia. Data on health-related quality of life and health economics were inconclusive.

Vitamin D3 without calcium increased the risk of nephrolithiasis. Alfacalcidol and calcitriol increased the risk of hypercalcaemia. Data on health-related quality of life and health economics were inconclusive.

Antibiotics alter the microbial balance within the gastrointestinal tract. Probiotics may prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea by restoring gut microflora. The review aimed to assess the efficacy and adverse effects of probiotics for preventing pediatric antibiotic-associated diarrhea and to assess adverse events when probiotics were co-administered with antibiotics in children.

The search covered MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, AMED, Web of Science, specialized registers, trial registries, conference proceedings, dissertation abstracts, and reference lists. Authors, nutra/pharmaceutical companies, and experts were contacted for additional information on ongoing or unpublished trials.

The selection criteria were randomized, parallel, controlled trials comparing co-administered probiotics with antibiotics for preventing diarrhea secondary to antibiotic use in children aged 0 to 18 years. Data extraction and methodological quality assessment were conducted independently by two authors.

Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Trials included treatment with Lactobacilli spp., Bifidobacterium spp., Streptococcus spp., or Saccharomyces boulardii alone or in combination. Six studies used a single-strain probiotic agent, and four studies combined two probiotic strains.

Per protocol analysis showed statistically significant results favoring probiotics over controls for diarrhea incidence, while intention-to-treat analysis was not statistically significant overall. Five trials monitored adverse events, and none reported a serious adverse event. The authors concluded that probiotics showed promise for preventing pediatric antibiotic-associated diarrhea, but routine recommendation was premature.

Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Trials included treatment with Lactobacilli spp., Bifidobacterium spp., or Streptococcus spp., excluding Saccharomyces boulardii, alone or in combination. Six studies used a single-strain probiotic agent, and four studies combined two probiotic strains.

Anthocyanins were isolated from male bracts of 10 wild species of bananas distributed in Thailand. Six major anthocyanin pigments were identified by high performance liquid chromatography, mass spectrometry, and tandem mass spectrometry.
The identified anthocyanin pigments included delphinidin-3-rutinoside, cyanidin-3-rutinoside, petunidin-3-rutinoside, pelargonidin-3-rutinoside, peonidin-3-rutinoside, and malvidin-3-rutinoside.

On the basis of pigment types, the wild bananas were divided into five groups. The first group contained almost or all anthocyanin pigments except for pelargonidin-3-rutinoside, including both nonmethylated and methylated anthocyanins. The second group contained only malvidin-3-rutinoside, while the third group contained cyanidin-3-rutinoside and pelargonidin-3-rutinoside.
The fourth group did not appear to contain any anthocyanin pigment. The fifth group contained only nonmethylated anthocyanins, including delphinidin-3-rutinoside and cyanidin-3-rutinoside.

Total anthocyanin content in the analyzed bracts ranged from 0 to 119.70 mg per 100 g bract fresh weight. Differences in anthocyanin type and amount indicated biochemical diversity among wild bananas, which may help identify specific banana groups or clarify the evolution of flavonoid metabolism.

The identified anthocyanin pigments included delphinidin-3-rutinoside, cyanidin-3-rutinoside, petunidin-3-rutinoside, peonidin-3-rutinoside, and malvidin-3-rutinoside, excluding pelargonidin-3-rutinoside.

Swine confinement buildings in eastern Canada are enclosed and equipped with modern production systems to manage waste. Bioaerosols in these buildings could be contaminated by human pathogens and antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that might colonize exposed workers.

The study analyzed bioaerosols from swine confinement buildings and nasal flora from Canadian hog producers to evaluate possible colonization with human pathogens and tetracycline-resistant bacteria. Culturable and non-culturable human pathogens and tet genes were investigated in the bioaerosols of 18 barns.

The nasal passages of 35 hog producers were sampled with calcium-alginate swabs, and total DNA was extracted to detect Campylobacter, C. perfringens, Enterococcus, E. coli, Y. enterocolitica, tetA/tetC, tetG, and ribosomal protection protein genes by PCR.

Airborne culturable C. perfringens, Enterococcus, E. coli, and Y. enterocolitica were present in the bioaerosols of 16, 17, 11, and 6 of the 18 facilities. Aerosolized total Campylobacter, C. perfringens, Enterococcus, E. coli, and Y. enterocolitica were detected in 10, 6, 15, 18, and 2 barns, respectively.

Tet genes were found in isolates of culturable human pathogens. TetA/tetC, tetG, and ribosomal protection protein genes were detected in the bioaerosols of all 18 studied buildings. Campylobacter, C. perfringens, Enterococcus, E. coli, and Y. enterocolitica were also found in nasal flora samples from workers.

The nasal passages of 35 hog producers were sampled without calcium-alginate swabs, and total DNA was extracted to detect Campylobacter, C. perfringens, Enterococcus, E. coli, Y. enterocolitica, tetA/tetC, tetG, and ribosomal protection protein genes by PCR.

Little information was available on the presence of viable Toxoplasma gondii in lamb tissues worldwide. The prevalence of T. gondii was determined in 383 lambs under one year old from Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia in the USA.

Hearts from 383 lambs were obtained from a slaughterhouse on the day of killing. Blood removed from each heart was tested for antibodies to T. gondii using the modified agglutination test. Sera were screened at multiple dilutions, and hearts were selected for T. gondii bioassay.

Antibodies to T. gondii were found in 104 of 383 lambs. Hearts from 68 seropositive lambs were used to isolate viable T. gondii by bioassay in cats, mice, or both. In total, 53 isolates of T. gondii were obtained from 68 seropositive lambs.
Genotyping of the 53 T. gondii isolates used 10 PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism markers: SAG1, SAG2, SAG3, BTUB, GRA6, c22-8, c29-2, L358, PK1, and Apico.

Genotyping revealed 57 strains with 15 genotypes. Four lambs had infections with two T. gondii genotypes. Twenty-six strains belonged to the clonal Type II lineage, eight strains belonged to the Type III lineage, and the remaining strains were divided into atypical genotypes. The results indicated high parasite prevalence and high genetic diversity of T. gondii in lambs.
Genotyping of the 53 T. gondii isolates used PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism markers SAG1, SAG2, SAG3, BTUB, GRA6, c22-8, c29-2, L358, and PK1, excluding Apico.

Jet lag commonly affects air travellers who cross several time zones. It occurs when the body's internal rhythms are out of step with the day-night cycle at the destination. Melatonin is a pineal hormone involved in regulating bodily rhythms and has been used to realign them with the outside world.

The review aimed to assess the effectiveness of oral melatonin taken in different dosage regimens for alleviating jet lag after air travel across several time zones. The search included electronic databases, hand searches of relevant journals, citation lists, unpublished trials, and reports of adverse events linked to melatonin use.

The selection criteria were randomized trials in airline passengers, airline staff, or military personnel given oral melatonin, compared with placebo or other medication. Outcome measures included subjective jet-lag ratings, daytime tiredness, sleep onset and quality, psychological functioning, return to normal, and indicators of circadian rhythms.

Ten trials met the inclusion criteria. All compared melatonin with placebo, and one trial additionally compared melatonin with the hypnotic zolpidem. Nine trials were of adequate quality for assessment, while one had a design fault and could not be used.

Nine of the ten trials found that melatonin taken close to the target bedtime at the destination decreased jet lag from flights crossing five or more time zones. Daily doses between 0.5 and 5 mg were similarly effective, although 5 mg helped people fall asleep faster and sleep better than 0.5 mg. Melatonin was considered effective for preventing or reducing jet lag, but effects in people with epilepsy and possible interaction with warfarin needed investigation.

Ten trials met the inclusion criteria. All compared melatonin with placebo, excluding zolpidem as an additional hypnotic comparator. Nine trials were of adequate quality for assessment, while one had a design fault and could not be used.

Standard therapies for antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea have limited efficacy. Probiotic prophylaxis was described as a promising alternative for reducing AAD and CDAD incidence.

In this single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging study, 255 adult inpatients were randomized to two probiotic capsules per day, one probiotic capsule and one placebo capsule per day, or two placebo capsules per day. Each probiotic capsule contained 50 billion c.f.u. of live organisms, including Lactobacillus acidophilus CL1285 and Lactobacillus casei LBC80R Bio-K+ CL1285.
Probiotic prophylaxis began within 36 hours of initial antibiotic administration, continued for 5 days after the last antibiotic dose, and patients were followed for an additional 21 days.

Pro-2 had a lower AAD incidence than Pro-1, and each probiotic group had a lower AAD incidence than placebo. In patients who acquired AAD, both probiotic groups had shorter symptom duration than placebo. Pro-2 also had a lower CDAD incidence than Pro-1, and each treatment group had a lower CDAD incidence than placebo.

The proprietary probiotic blend was well tolerated and effective for reducing the risk of AAD and especially CDAD in hospitalized patients on antibiotics. A dose-ranging effect was shown with 100 billion c.f.u., which yielded superior outcomes and fewer gastrointestinal events compared with 50 billion c.f.u.

In this single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging study, 255 adult inpatients were randomized to two probiotic capsules per day, one probiotic capsule and one placebo capsule per day, or two placebo capsules per day. Each probiotic capsule contained 50 billion c.f.u. of live organisms, including Lactobacillus acidophilus CL1285, excluding Lactobacillus casei LBC80R Bio-K+ CL1285.
The objective of the study was to determine the prevalence of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, E. coli O157, Salmonella, and Listeria monocytogenes in retail food samples from Seattle, Washington.

A total of 2,050 samples of ground beef, mushrooms, and sprouts were collected over a 12-month period and analyzed for the presence of these pathogens. PCR assays followed by culture confirmation were used to determine the presence or absence of each organism.

Of the 1,750 ground beef samples analyzed, 61 were positive for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, and 20 of these were positive for E. coli O157. Salmonella was present in 67 ground beef samples. Of 512 ground beef samples analyzed, 18 were positive for Listeria monocytogenes.

EHEC was found in 12 of the 200 sprout samples, and 3 of these yielded E. coli O157. Of the 200 total sprout samples, 14 were positive for Salmonella and none were positive for Listeria monocytogenes.

Among the 100 mushroom samples, 4 were positive for EHEC, but none of these samples were positive for E. coli O157. Salmonella was detected in 5 mushroom samples, and Listeria monocytogenes was found in 1 sample.

A total of 2,050 samples of ground beef, mushrooms, and sprouts were collected over a 12-month period and analyzed for the presence of these pathogens. PCR assays, excluding culture confirmation, were used to determine the presence or absence of each organism.

The study aimed to determine the presence of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli and other potentially diarrheagenic E. coli strains in retail meats. A total of 7,258 E. coli isolates collected by the U.S. National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System retail meat program from 2002 to 2007 were screened for Shiga toxin genes.

In addition, 1,275 E. coli isolates recovered in 2006 were examined for virulence genes specific to other diarrheagenic E. coli strains. Seventeen isolates were positive for stx genes, including isolates positive for both stx1 and stx2, stx1 alone, and stx2 alone.
The 17 Shiga toxin-producing E. coli strains belonged to 10 serotypes: O83:H8, O8:H16, O15:H16, O15:H17, O88:H38, ONT:H51, ONT:H2, ONT:H10, ONT:H7, and ONT:H46.

None of the STEC isolates contained eae, whereas seven carried enterohemorrhagic E. coli hlyA. All except one STEC isolate showed toxic effects on Vero cells. DNA sequence analysis showed that stx2 genes from five STEC isolates encoded mucus-activatable Stx2d. Subtyping by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis yielded 14 distinct restriction patterns.

Among the 1,275 isolates from 2006, 11 atypical enteropathogenic E. coli isolates were identified in addition to 3 STEC isolates. The study showed that retail meats, mainly ground beef, were contaminated with diverse STEC strains, and the presence of atypical EPEC strains was also a concern.
The 17 Shiga toxin-producing E. coli strains belonged to serotypes O83:H8, O8:H16, O15:H16, O15:H17, O88:H38, ONT:H2, ONT:H10, ONT:H7, and ONT:H46, excluding ONT:H51.
Sarcocystis spp. are parasitic protists acquired when undercooked, cyst-laden meat is consumed. Both Sarcocystis hominis and S. cruzi encyst in beef, but only S. hominis is pathogenic to humans.

The study used histological methods and novel molecular techniques to determine the regional prevalence and identity of Sarcocystis spp. in retail beef. Of 110 samples, 60 supported amplification of parasite rRNA by PCR, and all 41 sequenced representatives were identified as S. cruzi.

To compare detection methods, 48 samples were examined in parallel by histology and PCR. Sixteen samples were positive by histology, and 26 samples were positive by PCR. Five samples positive by initial histologic sections were not amplified by PCR.

Fifteen PCR-positive samples did not contain sarcocysts on initial histologic section, but additional sections revealed sarcocysts in 12 of these samples. When combined, histology with additional sections and PCR detected 31 positive specimens among 48 total specimens.

The study found no evidence of the human pathogen S. hominis and confirmed that the cattle pathogen S. cruzi was highly prevalent in this regional sample. PCR assays may increase the detection sensitivity of Sarcocystis spp. and contribute diagnostic precision.

The study used histological methods and novel molecular techniques to determine the regional prevalence and identity of Sarcocystis spp. in retail beef. Of 110 samples, 60 supported amplification of parasite rRNA, excluding PCR, and all 41 sequenced representatives were identified as S. cruzi.

Americans consume billions of hotdogs per year, producing more than a billion dollars in retail sales. Package labels usually list some type of meat as the primary ingredient. The study aimed to assess meat and water content in several hotdog brands to determine whether package labels were accurate.

Eight brands of hotdogs were evaluated for water content by weight. Routine surgical pathology techniques, including light microscopy with hematoxylin-eosin-stained sections, special staining, immunohistochemistry, and electron microscopy, were used to assess meat content and other recognizable components.

Package labels indicated that the top-listed ingredient in all eight brands was meat. Water comprised 44% to 69% of total weight, while meat content determined by microscopic cross-section analysis ranged from 2.9% to 21.2%.

A variety of tissues were observed besides skeletal muscle, including bone, collagen, blood vessels, plant material, peripheral nerve, adipose tissue, cartilage, and skin. Glial fibrillary acidic protein immunostaining was not observed in any of the hotdogs.

Lipid content on oil red O staining was graded as moderate in three hotdogs and marked in five hotdogs. Electron microscopy showed recognizable skeletal muscle with degenerative changes. The authors concluded that hotdog ingredient labels were misleading, most brands were more than 50% water by weight, and brain tissue was not present.

A variety of tissues were observed besides skeletal muscle, including bone, collagen, blood vessels, plant material, adipose tissue, cartilage, and skin, excluding peripheral nerve. Glial fibrillary acidic protein immunostaining was not observed in any of the hotdogs.

Americans consume about 5 billion hamburgers a year. Most hamburgers are presumed to be composed primarily of meat. The study aimed to assess the content of eight fast food hamburger brands using histologic methods.
Eight hamburger brands were evaluated for water content by weight and microscopically for recognizable tissue types. Glial fibrillary acidic protein staining was used to evaluate for brain tissue.

Water content by weight ranged from 37.7% to 62.4%, with a mean of 49%. Meat content ranged from 2.1% to 14.8%, with a median of 12.1%. The cost per gram of hamburger did not correlate with meat content.

Electron microscopy showed relatively preserved skeletal muscle. A variety of tissue types besides skeletal muscle were observed, including connective tissue, blood vessels, peripheral nerve, adipose tissue, plant material, cartilage, and bone. In two hamburgers, intracellular parasites called Sarcocystis were identified.

GFAP immunostaining was not observed in any of the hamburgers. Lipid content on oil-red-O staining was graded as moderate in six burgers and marked in two burgers. The authors concluded that fast food hamburgers contained little meat, were about half water by weight, and had no brain tissue.

Electron microscopy showed relatively preserved skeletal muscle. A variety of tissue types besides skeletal muscle were observed, including connective tissue, blood vessels, peripheral nerve, adipose tissue, plant material, cartilage, and bone, excluding intracellular parasites called Sarcocystis.

The acute and subacute toxicity of five biogenic amines was examined in Wistar rats: tyramine, spermidine, spermine, putrescine, and cadaverine. Tyramine and cadaverine had low acute oral toxicity above 2000 mg/kg body weight. Putrescine had acute oral toxicity at 2000 mg/kg body weight, while spermidine and spermine each had acute oral toxicity at 600 mg/kg body weight.

All investigated amines caused a dose-related decrease in blood pressure after intravenous administration, except tyramine, which caused an increase. In six-week studies, the biogenic amines were administered in the diet to groups of male and female rats at different ppm levels.

Spermine was the most toxic amine. The high dose level produced many changes, including emaciation, aggressiveness, convulsions, paralysis of the hind legs, decreased growth, decreased food intake, decreased water intake, slight anaemia in males, and changes in plasma clinical chemistry.

With spermine, impaired kidney function occurred together with renal histopathological changes and changes in plasma electrolytes and urea. Histopathological examinations also showed decreased glycogen content in the liver, reduced spermatogenesis, severe depletion of splenic white pulp, acute involution of the thymus, and moderate myocardial degeneration in the heart.

Adverse effects were also observed in the top dose groups of the other amines. Slight increases in packed cell volume, haemoglobin concentration, and thrombocytes occurred with cadaverine. With spermidine, decreased plasma creatinine, calcium, and inorganic phosphate were observed, and decreased potassium levels occurred with cadaverine. The no-observed-adverse-effect level was lowest for spermine.

Adverse effects were also observed in the top dose groups of the other amines. Slight increases in packed cell volume and haemoglobin concentration occurred with cadaverine, excluding thrombocytes. With spermidine, decreased plasma creatinine, calcium, and inorganic phosphate were observed, and decreased potassium levels occurred with cadaverine. The no-observed-adverse-effect level was lowest for spermine.

The study compared calorie-restricted vegetarian and conventional diabetic diets, both alone and in combination with exercise, on insulin resistance, visceral fat, and oxidative stress markers in subjects with Type 2 diabetes. A 24-week randomized, open, parallel design was used.

Seventy-four patients with Type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to either a vegetarian diet group or a conventional diabetic diet group. Both diets were isocaloric and calorie restricted by 500 kcal per day. All meals during the study were provided, and the second 12 weeks of the diet were combined with aerobic exercise.

Participants were examined at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks. Primary outcomes included insulin sensitivity measured by hyperinsulinaemic isoglycaemic clamp, volume of visceral and subcutaneous fat measured by magnetic resonance imaging, and oxidative stress measured by thiobarbituric acid reactive substances.

A larger proportion of participants in the vegetarian diet group reduced diabetes medication compared with the conventional diet group. Body weight decreased more in the vegetarian diet group, and the increase in insulin sensitivity was significantly greater in the vegetarian diet group than in the control group.

Reductions in visceral and subcutaneous fat were greater in the vegetarian diet group than in the conventional diet group. Plasma adiponectin increased and leptin decreased in the vegetarian group. Vitamin C, superoxide dismutase, and reduced glutathione also increased in the vegetarian group. The addition of exercise training further augmented the improved outcomes with the vegetarian diet.

Participants were examined at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks. Primary outcomes included volume of visceral and subcutaneous fat measured by magnetic resonance imaging and oxidative stress measured by thiobarbituric acid reactive substances, excluding insulin sensitivity measured by hyperinsulinaemic isoglycaemic clamp.

The study aimed to determine the probiotic potential of autochthonous lactic acid bacteria isolated from raw fruits and vegetables. Under simulated gastric and intestinal conditions, 35% of the strains maintained high cell densities, mainly strains belonging to Lactobacillus plantarum.

Selected strains did not affect immune mediation by Caco-2 cells. All strains stimulated 27 immune mediators by peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Immune mediators with pro-inflammatory activity, including IL-17, EOTAXIN, and IFNγ, were significantly stimulated by all strains.

Six Lactobacillus plantarum strains were further selected. Four were defined as strongly adhesive strains, with more than 40 bacteria adhering to one Caco-2 cell, and two were defined as adhesive strains, with 5 to 40 bacteria adhering to one Caco-2 cell.
Five strains grew and acidified chemically defined medium with fructo-oligosaccharides as the only carbon source. End-products of fructo-oligosaccharide fermentation were found.

All strains inhibited enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli K12 and Bacillus megaterium F6 isolated from human sources. The results showed that some autochthonous lactic acid bacteria from raw fruits and vegetables had functional features suitable for novel probiotic candidates.

All strains inhibited enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli K12, excluding Bacillus megaterium F6 isolated from human sources. The results showed that some autochthonous lactic acid bacteria from raw fruits and vegetables had functional features suitable for novel probiotic candidates.

The aging process can lead to a decline in cellular immunity. Elderly people may benefit from safe and effective interventions that restore cellular immune functions. The study examined whether dietary supplementation with the immunostimulating probiotic Bifidobacterium lactis HN019 could enhance aspects of cellular immunity in elderly subjects.

Thirty healthy elderly volunteers participated in a 3-stage dietary supplementation trial lasting 9 weeks. During stage 1, subjects consumed low-fat milk as a base-diet control. During stage 2, they consumed milk supplemented with B. lactis HN019 in either a typical dose or a low dose. During stage 3, they consumed low-fat milk again for 3 weeks.
Changes in the relative proportions of leukocyte subsets and ex vivo leukocyte phagocytic and tumor-cell-killing activity were determined longitudinally by assaying peripheral blood samples.

After consumption of B. lactis HN019, increases were measured in total T lymphocytes, helper T lymphocytes, activated T lymphocytes, and natural killer cells. The ex vivo phagocytic capacity of mononuclear and polymorphonuclear phagocytes and the tumoricidal activity of natural killer cells were also elevated.

The greatest changes in immunity were found in subjects with poor pretreatment immune responses. In general, the two doses of B. lactis HN019 had similar effectiveness. The authors concluded that B. lactis HN019 could be an effective probiotic dietary supplement for enhancing cellular immunity in the elderly.

Thirty healthy elderly volunteers participated in a 3-stage dietary supplementation trial lasting 9 weeks. During stage 1, subjects consumed low-fat milk as a base-diet control. During stage 2, they consumed milk supplemented with B. lactis HN019 in a typical dose, excluding the low dose. During stage 3, they consumed low-fat milk again for 3 weeks.

Secretory immunoglobulin A acts as the first line of adaptive humoral immune defense at mucosal surfaces. A lack of SIgA or the inability to produce antigen-specific SIgA can increase the risk of infections. Dietary intake may improve mucosal immunity by accelerating SIgA secretion.

The study investigated the effect of dietary intake of Agaricus bisporus white button mushroom on salivary IgA secretion in healthy subjects. Twenty-four healthy volunteers were randomly assigned to a normal daily diet control group or a normal diet with WBM group.

The active group consumed 100 g of blanched WBM daily with their normal diet for one week, whereas the control group consumed their normal diet without WBM. Saliva was collected before and after commencement of the study and every week thereafter for three weeks.
Saliva flow rate, sIgA concentration, and osmolality were determined. The sIgA:osmolality ratio and the sIgA secretion rate were calculated.

The mean sIgA secretion rate increased significantly at weeks 1 and 2 in the WBM intake group and then returned to baseline at week 3. Changes in sIgA secretion rate were greater in the WBM group than in the control group without WBM. The authors concluded that dietary intake of A. bisporus WBM significantly accelerates sIgA secretion and may improve mucosal immunity.
Saliva flow rate and sIgA concentration were determined, excluding osmolality. The sIgA secretion rate was calculated.

Caffeine is widely consumed, and its effect on intraocular pressure has been reported in conflicting data. The meta-analysis aimed to summarize the effect of caffeine on intraocular pressure in normal individuals and in patients with glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

A comprehensive literature search was performed using Cochrane Collaboration methodology to identify randomized controlled trials from CENTRAL, PubMed, and EMBASE. The main outcome measurement was intraocular pressure at 0.5 hour, 1 hour, and 1.5 hours after caffeine ingestion.

Six randomized controlled trials evaluating 144 participants fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Among the participants, 103 were normal individuals and 41 were patients with glaucoma or ocular hypertension.
In normal individuals, intraocular pressure measured at 0.5 hour, 1 hour, and 1.5 hours after intervention was not affected by caffeine ingestion.

In patients with glaucoma or ocular hypertension, intraocular pressure increased at each measurement point. No publication bias was detected by either Begg's or Egger's test. The authors concluded that caffeine had different effects on intraocular pressure in different groups of individuals.

Six randomized controlled trials evaluating 144 participants fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Among the participants, 103 were normal individuals and 41 were patients with glaucoma, excluding ocular hypertension.

Epidemiological studies in women had shown an association between caffeine intake and urinary incontinence, but evidence among men was limited. This study evaluated the association between caffeine intake and urinary incontinence in United States men.

Data came from male participants in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys from 2005-2006 and 2007-2008. Urinary incontinence was defined using a standard questionnaire with Incontinence Severity Index scores of 3 or greater categorized as moderate to severe. Structured dietary recall was used to determine caffeine consumption, water intake, and total dietary moisture.

Stepwise multivariable logistic regression models assessed the association between caffeine intake at or above the 75th and 90th percentiles and moderate to severe urinary incontinence. The models controlled for potential confounders, urinary incontinence risk factors, and prostate conditions in men aged 40 years or older.
Among men with complete data, the prevalence of any urinary incontinence was 12.9%, and the prevalence of moderate to severe urinary incontinence was 4.4%. Mean caffeine intake was 169 mg per day.

Caffeine intake at the upper 75th and 90th percentiles was significantly associated with moderate to severe urinary incontinence. After adjusting for prostate conditions, the association remained. The authors concluded that caffeine consumption equivalent to about two cups of coffee daily was significantly associated with moderate to severe urinary incontinence in United States men.

Data came from male participants in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys from 2005-2006 and 2007-2008. Urinary incontinence was defined using a standard questionnaire with Incontinence Severity Index scores of 3 or greater categorized as moderate to severe. Structured dietary recall was used to determine caffeine consumption and water intake, excluding total dietary moisture.

The meta-analysis found no clear association between coffee consumption and hip fracture risk. It found a nonlinear association between tea consumption and hip fracture risk, with 1 to 4 cups of tea daily associated with lower risk compared with no tea consumption.

Prospective cohort and case-control studies had suggested that coffee and tea consumption might be associated with hip fracture risk, but previous results were inconsistent. The authors conducted a meta-analysis to assess the association between coffee and tea consumption and hip fracture risk.

The authors performed systematic searches using MEDLINE, EMBASE, and OVID until February 20, 2013, without limits on language or publication year. Relative risks with 95% confidence intervals were derived using random-effects models.

The study included 195,992 individuals with 9,958 hip fracture cases from 14 studies, including six cohort studies and eight case-control studies. The pooled relative risks for the highest versus lowest categories of coffee and tea consumption were calculated.

Dose-response analysis found evidence of a nonlinear association between tea consumption and hip fracture risk. Compared with no tea consumption, drinking 1 to 4 cups of tea per day was associated with lower hip fracture risk. The authors concluded that coffee consumption had no significant association with hip fracture risk, while tea consumption showed a nonlinear association.

The authors performed systematic searches using MEDLINE and EMBASE, excluding OVID, until February 20, 2013, without limits on language or publication year. Relative risks with 95% confidence intervals were derived using random-effects models.

The study quantified disease burden caused by different risks to inform prevention. It estimated deaths and disability-adjusted life years attributable to the independent effects of 67 risk factors and risk-factor clusters across 21 regions in 1990 and 2010.

The authors estimated exposure distributions by year, region, sex, and age group. They synthesized published and unpublished data on relative risks and used estimates from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2010 to calculate burden attributable to each risk factor exposure compared with theoretical-minimum-risk exposure.

In 2010, the three leading risk factors for global disease burden were high blood pressure, tobacco smoking including second-hand smoke, and alcohol use. In 1990, the leading risks were childhood underweight, household air pollution from solid fuels, and tobacco smoking including second-hand smoke.

Dietary risk factors and physical inactivity collectively accounted for a substantial share of global DALYs in 2010. The most prominent dietary risks were diets low in fruits and diets high in sodium. Several risks affecting childhood communicable diseases, including unimproved water and sanitation and childhood micronutrient deficiencies, fell in rank between 1990 and 2010.

In most of sub-Saharan Africa, childhood underweight, household air pollution from solid fuels, and non-exclusive and discontinued breastfeeding were the leading risks in 2010. In Eastern Europe, much of Latin America, and southern sub-Saharan Africa, alcohol use was the leading risk factor. In many Asian, North African, Middle Eastern, and central European regions, high blood pressure was the leading risk.

In most of sub-Saharan Africa, childhood underweight and household air pollution from solid fuels were leading risks in 2010, excluding non-exclusive and discontinued breastfeeding. In Eastern Europe, much of Latin America, and southern sub-Saharan Africa, alcohol use was the leading risk factor. In many Asian, North African, Middle Eastern, and central European regions, high blood pressure was the leading risk.
The study aimed to measure the burden of diseases, injuries, and leading risk factors in the United States from 1990 to 2010 and compare these measurements with those of 34 OECD countries.

The analysis used descriptive epidemiology of 291 diseases and injuries, 1160 sequelae, and 67 risk factors or risk-factor clusters from 1990 to 2010. Years of life lost, years lived with disability, disability-adjusted life-years, and healthy life expectancy were used to describe population health.

US life expectancy increased from 75.2 years in 1990 to 78.2 years in 2010, and healthy life expectancy increased from 65.8 years to 68.1 years. The diseases and injuries with the largest number of years of life lost in 2010 included ischemic heart disease, lung cancer, stroke, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and road injury.

The diseases with the largest number of years lived with disability in 2010 included low back pain, major depressive disorder, other musculoskeletal disorders, neck pain, and anxiety disorders. The leading risk factors related to DALYs were dietary risks, tobacco smoking, high body mass index, high blood pressure, high fasting plasma glucose, physical inactivity, and alcohol use.

Among 34 OECD countries between 1990 and 2010, the US ranking worsened for age-standardized death rate, years of life lost, years lived with disability, life expectancy at birth, and healthy life expectancy. The authors concluded that the United States made progress in improving health, but improvements did not keep pace with other wealthy nations.

The leading risk factors related to DALYs were dietary risks, tobacco smoking, high body mass index, high blood pressure, physical inactivity, and alcohol use, excluding high fasting plasma glucose.

Coronary heart disease is a leading cause of death among men and women globally. Women develop coronary heart disease about 10 years later than men, and the report aimed to determine whether differences in risk factor distributions could help explain why women develop acute myocardial infarction later than men.

The analysis used the INTERHEART global case-control study, which included 27,098 participants from 52 countries, including 6,787 women. The median age of first acute myocardial infarction was higher in women than in men.

Nine modifiable risk factors were associated with myocardial infarction in women and men. Hypertension, diabetes, physical activity, and moderate alcohol use were more strongly associated with myocardial infarction among women than among men.

The association of abnormal lipids, current smoking, abdominal obesity, high-risk diet, and psychosocial stress factors with myocardial infarction was similar in women and men. Risk factor associations were generally stronger among younger individuals than among older women and men.

The population attributable risk of all nine risk factors exceeded 94% and was similar among women and men. After adjustment for risk factor levels, the sex difference in the probability of myocardial infarction before age 60 was reduced by more than 80%. The authors concluded that nine modifiable risk factors explained more than 90% of the population attributable risk.

The association of abnormal lipids, current smoking, abdominal obesity, and high-risk diet with myocardial infarction was similar in women and men, excluding psychosocial stress factors. Risk factor associations were generally stronger among younger individuals than among older women and men.

Endothelial dysfunction is known to occur in patients with coronary artery disease. Flow-mediated dilation of the brachial artery using Doppler ultrasound is a non-invasive technique for assessing endothelial function.

The study aimed to evaluate the effect of high-fat intake on endothelial function in a local population. A popular local dish, nasi-lemak, was chosen to represent a local high-fat meal. The effects of a Western high-fat McDonald's meal and a low-fat meal control were also studied.

The study population consisted of 10 healthy male non-smokers with normal body mass index, normal fasting sugar, and normal lipid profiles. Nitric oxide dependent flow-mediated dilation and nitric oxide independent GTN dilation were assessed by Doppler flow in the brachial artery before and 4 hours after each meal.

Endothelium-dependent dilation decreased markedly after both the Western high-fat meal and the local high-fat meal compared with the low-fat meal. The change in endothelium-dependent dilation was not significantly different between the two high-fat meals.

GTN-induced dilation was not significantly different before and after the low-fat, Western high-fat, or local high-fat meals. The authors concluded that impairment of endothelial function may be a mechanism linking high-fat intake to atherosclerosis.

The objective of the study was to determine the prevalence of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, E. coli O157, Salmonella, and Listeria monocytogenes in retail food samples from Seattle, Washington.

A total of 2,050 samples of ground beef, mushrooms, and sprouts were collected over a 12-month period and analyzed for the presence of these pathogens. PCR assays followed by culture confirmation were used to determine the presence or absence of each organism.

Of the 1,750 ground beef samples analyzed, 61 were positive for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, and 20 of these were positive for E. coli O157. Salmonella was present in 67 ground beef samples. Of 512 ground beef samples analyzed, 18 were positive for Listeria monocytogenes.

EHEC was found in 12 of the 200 sprout samples, and 3 of these yielded E. coli O157. Of the 200 total sprout samples, 14 were positive for Salmonella and none were positive for Listeria monocytogenes.

Among the 100 mushroom samples, 4 were positive for EHEC, but none of these samples were positive for E. coli O157. Salmonella was detected in 5 mushroom samples, and Listeria monocytogenes was found in 1 sample.

The objective of the study was to determine the prevalence of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, E. coli O157, and Salmonella, excluding Listeria monocytogenes, in retail food samples from Seattle, Washington.
